rewrites.change_summary: swap d3 (fabricated cross-region 'silently disabled' constraint) -> DNS TTL caching, a real failover-delay cause that is wrong here

before.question: You configure a Route 53 failover routing policy with a primary record pointing to a regional ALB and a secondary record pointing to a static S3 website. The primary ALB starts returning 500s but Route 53 keeps sending traffic to it. Why?

options.correct: Failover routing relies on a Route 53 health check on the primary; if no health check is associated, Route 53 always answers with the primary regardless of its actual health
options.distractor_1: Route 53 detects application errors via ALB target group health, which the failover policy reads automatically
options.distractor_2: Failover only triggers on DNS resolution failures; 500 status codes are above the DNS layer and Route 53 ignores them by design
options.distractor_3: Failover routing requires the secondary to be in a different AWS region; same-region secondaries are silently disabled

before.explanation: Failover routing is driven by Route 53 health checks attached to the primary record — without one, there's nothing to flip on. Distractor 1 conflates Route 53 with the ALB target group's own health checks; ALB knows its targets are unhealthy but Route 53 doesn't until you point a health check at the ALB. Distractor 2 (DNS-failure trigger) misdescribes failover entirely — Route 53 health checks run HTTP/HTTPS probes against the endpoint. Distractor 3 invents a cross-region constraint; failover works across any record types in any region.

after.question: You configure a Route 53 failover routing policy with a primary record pointing to a regional ALB and a secondary record pointing to a static S3 website. The primary ALB starts returning 500s but Route 53 keeps sending traffic to it. Why?

options.correct: Failover routing relies on a Route 53 health check on the primary; if no health check is associated, Route 53 always answers with the primary regardless of its actual health
options.distractor_1: Route 53 detects application errors via ALB target group health, which the failover policy reads automatically
options.distractor_2: Failover only triggers on DNS resolution failures; 500 status codes are above the DNS layer and Route 53 ignores them by design
options.distractor_3: The DNS record's TTL hasn't expired yet, so resolvers are still returning the cached primary record even though Route 53 has already failed over at its end

after.explanation: Failover routing is driven by Route 53 health checks attached to the primary record — without one, there's nothing to flip on. Distractor 1 conflates Route 53 with the ALB target group's own health checks; ALB knows its targets are unhealthy but Route 53 doesn't until you point a health check at the ALB. Distractor 2 (DNS-failure trigger) misdescribes failover entirely — Route 53 health checks run HTTP/HTTPS probes against the endpoint. Distractor 3 reaches for DNS TTL caching — a real failover-delay cause — but here Route 53 never flipped at all (no health check is attached), so there's nothing cached to expire.

distractor_self_check.real_misconception: DNS TTL caching genuinely delays failover; a junior who knows DNS caching would reach for it, but with no health check Route 53 never failed over, so nothing is cached.

rewrites.change_summary: swap all three distractors (all were fabricated post-resize mechanisms) -> cold page cache, per-core clock/contention, bandwidth-split misconceptions

before.question: An EC2 instance running at 95% CPU prompts a team to switch from m5.large to m5.xlarge. After the change, CPU drops to 50% but the application is now slower. What's the most likely cause?

options.correct: CPU wasn't the real bottleneck; the larger instance let the actual constraint (memory, disk I/O, network) saturate faster
options.distractor_1: EC2 instance scaling has a one-hour stabilisation period during which CPU is artificially limited
options.distractor_2: Moving up an instance class introduces a multi-hour kernel warm-tuning period during which performance regresses before returning to baseline
options.distractor_3: m5.xlarge uses a different Nitro generation that requires the AMI to be rebuilt before performance returns to baseline

before.explanation: Right-sizing by CPU metric alone catches the wrong target when CPU is the symptom and not the cause. Increased capacity often unmasks an upstream bottleneck (a connection pool, disk queue, etc.) that now serves more concurrent work. Distractor 1 invents a stabilisation period. Distractor 2 invents a kernel warm-up phase. Distractor 3 fabricates a Nitro generation mismatch story; AMIs work across instance sizes within a family. The methodology lesson: combine CloudWatch with the application's own metrics before resizing.

after.question: An EC2 instance running at 95% CPU prompts a team to switch from m5.large to m5.xlarge. After the change, CPU drops to 50% but the application is now slower. What's the most likely cause?

options.correct: CPU wasn't the real bottleneck; the larger instance let the actual constraint (memory, disk I/O, network) saturate faster
options.distractor_1: The stop/start required to resize the instance cleared the OS page cache, so the application stays slow until its filesystem caches warm back up
options.distractor_2: m5.large and m5.xlarge run on the same hardware generation, but the larger size has more vCPUs at the same per-core clock, so any single-threaded hot path runs no faster and added lock contention can slow it
options.distractor_3: Doubling the vCPUs splits the instance's fixed network and EBS bandwidth across more cores, so per-core I/O throughput dropped after the resize

after.explanation: Right-sizing by CPU metric alone catches the wrong target when CPU is the symptom and not the cause. Increased capacity often unmasks an upstream bottleneck (a connection pool, disk queue, etc.) that now serves more concurrent work. Distractor 1 blames a cold page cache after the resize's stop/start — real, but transient, and it wouldn't explain sustained slowness at a steady 50% CPU. Distractor 2 assumes a slower per-core clock or lock contention — but m5.large and m5.xlarge share the same hardware and clock, and the app's own concurrency is the limiter. Distractor 3 inverts the bandwidth story — larger instances get more network and EBS bandwidth, not a split share. The methodology lesson: combine CloudWatch with the application's own metrics before resizing.

distractor_self_check.real_misconception: Resizing an EC2 instance requires a stop/start, which really does clear the page cache; a junior would attribute post-resize slowness to a cold cache, not realising it's transient.
Juniors commonly think more vCPUs means a slower per-core clock or more contention; m5.large/xlarge in fact share clock and hardware.
A natural but wrong 'fixed pool divided among more cores' model; AWS scales bandwidth up with instance size.

Distractor 2 invents an EKS scheduling overhead that doesn't exist (pod startup is seconds, not minutes). Distractor 3 ignores the constraint entirely. The general rule: Lambda for short, event-driven workloads; ECS/EKS for sustained or long-running.

rewrites.change_summary: swap d3 (fabricated CloudWatch billing event) -> belief that restart erases CloudWatch metric history

before.question: An EC2 instance shows 90% CPU. You see one process (java) consuming most of it. The team's first impulse is to restart it. Why might that be the wrong response?

options.correct: High CPU is a symptom, not a cause — restarting hides the underlying driver (a slow query, a JIT warmup loop, a real traffic spike) and you lose the diagnostic window
options.distractor_1: Restarting Java processes triggers a 60-second JVM cold-start period during which CPU spikes higher, making the situation worse
options.distractor_2: ASG would mark the instance unhealthy mid-restart and terminate it before the process recovers
options.distractor_3: Restarting the process triggers a CloudWatch billing event because of the metric stream interruption

before.explanation: Restart-first is the operational equivalent of unplugging the smoke alarm — the alarm stops but the fire continues. Capturing thread dumps, profiling the JIT, and correlating with upstream traffic teaches what to fix. Distractor 1 over-states JVM cold start; modern JVMs warm up in seconds, and the issue is diagnosis, not warm-up. Distractor 2 misrepresents ASG behaviour — process restart isn't an ASG event. Distractor 3 fabricates a billing penalty. The methodology lesson: always capture state before recovering.

after.question: An EC2 instance shows 90% CPU. You see one process (java) consuming most of it. The team's first impulse is to restart it. Why might that be the wrong response?

options.correct: High CPU is a symptom, not a cause — restarting hides the underlying driver (a slow query, a JIT warmup loop, a real traffic spike) and you lose the diagnostic window
options.distractor_1: Restarting Java processes triggers a 60-second JVM cold-start period during which CPU spikes higher, making the situation worse
options.distractor_2: ASG would mark the instance unhealthy mid-restart and terminate it before the process recovers
options.distractor_3: Restarting wipes the CloudWatch metric history for the instance, so you'd lose the record of the spike needed for the post-incident review

after.explanation: Restart-first is the operational equivalent of unplugging the smoke alarm — the alarm stops but the fire continues. Capturing thread dumps, profiling the JIT, and correlating with upstream traffic teaches what to fix. Distractor 1 over-states JVM cold start; modern JVMs warm up in seconds, and the issue is diagnosis, not warm-up. Distractor 2 misrepresents ASG behaviour — process restart isn't an ASG event. Distractor 3 assumes restarting erases CloudWatch history — but CloudWatch stores metrics as durable time-series independent of the process; what you actually lose by restarting is the live process state (thread dumps, the running JIT profile), not the recorded metrics. The methodology lesson: always capture state before recovering.

distractor_self_check.real_misconception: Juniors often think restarting erases monitoring data; CloudWatch retains metrics independently. A believable wrong reason that mirrors the correct 'lose the diagnostic window' but targets stored metrics, not live state.

rewrites.change_summary: swap d1 (fabricated 2023 deprecation) -> 'newer = less capable, no custom domains' misconception

before.question: You're choosing between API Gateway REST API and API Gateway HTTP API for a new serverless backend. Which is the more common right choice today and why?

options.correct: HTTP API — lower latency, ~70% cheaper, and covers what most teams need (JWT auth, CORS, Lambda integration)
options.distractor_1: REST API — HTTP API was deprecated in 2023 and is no longer recommended for new builds
options.distractor_2: REST API — HTTP API doesn't support Lambda integrations, which makes it unsuitable for most serverless backends
options.distractor_3: HTTP API — it's the only API Gateway type that supports VPC integrations, making it required for any private backend

before.explanation: HTTP API is the modern default: cheaper, faster, simpler, with the features most teams actually use. REST API still has a place when you need request validators, complex mappings, WAF, or private edge-optimised endpoints. Distractor 1 fabricates a deprecation. Distractor 2 inverts the truth — HTTP API supports Lambda integrations natively (in fact more cleanly than REST API). Distractor 3 misstates capability — both API types support VPC links / integrations.

after.question: You're choosing between API Gateway REST API and API Gateway HTTP API for a new serverless backend. Which is the more common right choice today and why?

options.correct: HTTP API — lower latency, ~70% cheaper, and covers what most teams need (JWT auth, CORS, Lambda integration)
options.distractor_1: REST API — it's the more mature option; HTTP API still doesn't support custom domain names or TLS certificates, so it can't serve production traffic on a branded endpoint
options.distractor_2: REST API — HTTP API doesn't support Lambda integrations, which makes it unsuitable for most serverless backends
options.distractor_3: HTTP API — it's the only API Gateway type that supports VPC integrations, making it required for any private backend

after.explanation: HTTP API is the modern default: cheaper, faster, simpler, with the features most teams actually use. REST API still has a place when you need request validators, complex mappings, WAF, or private edge-optimised endpoints. Distractor 1 leans on a 'newer means less capable' assumption — but HTTP API has supported custom domain names and ACM TLS certificates since launch, so the branded-endpoint objection is false. Distractor 2 inverts the truth — HTTP API supports Lambda integrations natively (in fact more cleanly than REST API). Distractor 3 misstates capability — both API types support VPC links / integrations.

distractor_self_check.real_misconception: A common 'the newer simpler option must lack enterprise features' assumption; HTTP API has supported custom domains and ACM certs from the start.

rewrites.change_summary: swap d1: drop the false 'CI speed scales linearly with size' absolute; keep the genuine at-bar 'bigger runner fixes slow CI' instinct

before.question: Your CI pipeline takes 25 minutes — too slow for the team's rapid commit cadence. Which optimisation gives the biggest realistic speedup?

options.correct: Parallelise independent stages (lint, unit tests, security scan) and shard slow test suites across multiple runners
options.distractor_1: Increase the runner's CPU and memory to the maximum tier; CI speed scales linearly with resource size
options.distractor_2: Skip the integration test stage on every PR and run it only on main branch merges, since it's the slowest stage
options.distractor_3: Switch from GitHub-hosted runners to a larger third-party runner provider with faster network throughput between runners

before.explanation: Parallelisation and sharding give 3-5x speedups on most pipelines because stages and tests are I/O-bound rather than CPU-bound. Distractor 1 over-promises — bigger runners help marginally if at all; serial test runs don't speed up with more CPU beyond a point. Distractor 2 reduces signal coverage (PRs would merge with integration failures) — wrong trade-off. Distractor 3 adds infrastructure cost without addressing the fundamental serial-vs-parallel issue.

after.question: Your CI pipeline takes 25 minutes — too slow for the team's rapid commit cadence. Which optimisation gives the biggest realistic speedup?

options.correct: Parallelise independent stages (lint, unit tests, security scan) and shard slow test suites across multiple runners
options.distractor_1: Upgrade to the largest available runner tier so the whole pipeline runs on more CPU and memory
options.distractor_2: Skip the integration test stage on every PR and run it only on main branch merges, since it's the slowest stage
options.distractor_3: Switch from GitHub-hosted runners to a larger third-party runner provider with faster network throughput between runners

after.explanation: Parallelisation and sharding give 3-5x speedups on most pipelines because stages and tests are I/O-bound rather than CPU-bound. Distractor 1 throws hardware at the problem — a real instinct, but most CI time is I/O-bound (dependency installs, network, serial test ordering), so a bigger runner barely moves a 25-minute pipeline; the win is parallelism, not raw size. Distractor 2 reduces signal coverage (PRs would merge with integration failures) — wrong trade-off. Distractor 3 adds infrastructure cost without addressing the fundamental serial-vs-parallel issue.

distractor_self_check.real_misconception: Throwing a bigger runner at slow CI is a near-universal junior instinct; it barely helps because pipelines are I/O-bound and serial. The 'scales linearly' over-claim is removed; the underlying misconception is at-bar.

rewrites.change_summary: swap d3 (fabricated COMPOSITE_ prefix convention) -> 'cross-repo actions are blocked from secrets' misconception

before.question: Your composite action needs access to a secret stored at the repository level. What's true about secrets and composite actions?

options.correct: Composite actions can read secrets passed as inputs from the calling workflow but cannot directly access repository secrets without explicit passthrough
options.distractor_1: Composite actions inherit all repository and organization secrets automatically without any explicit passing required
options.distractor_2: Composite actions cannot use secrets at all; secrets are restricted to job-level steps written directly in the workflow file
options.distractor_3: Composite actions can access secrets only when they're stored in the calling workflow's environment with name prefixed COMPOSITE_

before.explanation: Composite actions are sandboxed from secrets — the calling workflow must pass secrets as inputs explicitly (with `secrets:` context in a reusable workflow, or as input values for composite actions). Distractor 1 inverts the access model. Distractor 2 over-tightens — composite actions can use secrets, just via explicit passthrough. Distractor 3 invents a prefix convention that doesn't exist. This is the most common composite-action gotcha for teams refactoring from inline steps.

after.question: Your composite action needs access to a secret stored at the repository level. What's true about secrets and composite actions?

options.correct: Composite actions can read secrets passed as inputs from the calling workflow but cannot directly access repository secrets without explicit passthrough
options.distractor_1: Composite actions inherit all repository and organization secrets automatically without any explicit passing required
options.distractor_2: Composite actions cannot use secrets at all; secrets are restricted to job-level steps written directly in the workflow file
options.distractor_3: Composite actions can use secrets only if the action's YAML lives in the same repository as the calling workflow; actions referenced from another repository are blocked from all secrets

after.explanation: Composite actions are sandboxed from secrets — the calling workflow must pass secrets as inputs explicitly (with `secrets:` context in a reusable workflow, or as input values for composite actions). Distractor 1 inverts the access model. Distractor 2 over-tightens — composite actions can use secrets, just via explicit passthrough. Distractor 3 ties secret access to where the action lives — but a composite action receives secrets through explicit input passing regardless of which repository hosts it; location isn't the gate. This is the most common composite-action gotcha for teams refactoring from inline steps.

distractor_self_check.real_misconception: Juniors often assume third-party/cross-repo actions can't receive secrets; access depends on explicit passthrough, not action location.

rewrites.change_summary: swap d3 (invented skip-matrix: key) -> fail-fast:false, a real setting misapplied as 'skip a combo'

before.question: Your matrix has `os: [ubuntu, macos, windows]` and `node: [18, 20]` but you don't want the macos+node18 combination because it's flaky. How do you skip it?

options.correct: Use `exclude:` in the strategy with `{os: macos, node: 18}` to remove that one combination while keeping all others
options.distractor_1: Set `continue-on-error: true` on the specific matrix combination so its failures don't fail the workflow
options.distractor_2: Use `if: ${{ !(matrix.os == 'macos' && matrix.node == 18) }}` on every step inside the matrix job to make all steps no-ops for that combo
options.distractor_3: Add `skip-matrix:` to the workflow YAML with the combination key, which tells GitHub to not even queue that job run

before.explanation: The native solution is `exclude:` (and `include:` adds combinations beyond the cross-product). Distractor 1 keeps the job running and silences failures — wasteful and noisy. Distractor 2 keeps the job queued and runs through every step as a no-op — extreme overhead for skipping. Distractor 3 invents a `skip-matrix:` key that doesn't exist. Matrix pruning matters at scale — a 3×3×3 cross-product is 27 jobs, and `exclude:` keeps the bill in check.

after.question: Your matrix has `os: [ubuntu, macos, windows]` and `node: [18, 20]` but you don't want the macos+node18 combination because it's flaky. How do you skip it?

options.correct: Use `exclude:` in the strategy with `{os: macos, node: 18}` to remove that one combination while keeping all others
options.distractor_1: Set `continue-on-error: true` on the specific matrix combination so its failures don't fail the workflow
options.distractor_2: Use `if: ${{ !(matrix.os == 'macos' && matrix.node == 18) }}` on every step inside the matrix job to make all steps no-ops for that combo
options.distractor_3: Set `fail-fast: false` in the strategy so the flaky macos+node18 combination still runs but no longer cancels the other matrix jobs when it fails

after.explanation: The native solution is `exclude:` (and `include:` adds combinations beyond the cross-product). Distractor 1 keeps the job running and silences failures — wasteful and noisy. Distractor 2 keeps the job queued and runs through every step as a no-op — extreme overhead for skipping. Distractor 3 reaches for `fail-fast: false` — a real strategy setting, but it only stops one leg's failure from cancelling the others; the macos+node18 job still runs, so nothing is skipped. Matrix pruning matters at scale — a 3×3×3 cross-product is 27 jobs, and `exclude:` keeps the bill in check.

distractor_self_check.real_misconception: fail-fast: false is a real matrix setting; a junior confuses 'stop this combo breaking the build' with 'remove it,' when it only decouples sibling cancellation.

rewrites.change_summary: swap d1 (fabricated local-cache auto-sync) -> 'a pulled image is reused as build cache automatically' misconception

before.question: You build a Docker image in CI and want to reuse the layer cache across runs even though each runner is fresh. What pattern works?

options.correct: BuildKit with a registry-backed cache (`--cache-to type=registry --cache-from type=registry`) — layers live in a remote registry and are pulled on subsequent runs
options.distractor_1: BuildKit local cache (`--cache-to type=local`) — local caches are automatically synchronised across runners by GitHub Actions
options.distractor_2: Docker Hub's persistent layer storage — every image tag pushed to Docker Hub seeds the layer cache for all future builds in the same org
options.distractor_3: Compressed tar of the Docker daemon storage directory uploaded as a build artifact — restored at the start of each subsequent run

before.explanation: Registry cache is the standard pattern: BuildKit pushes the build cache to a registry (often the same one as the image), and pulls it on the next run. The runner can be fresh because the cache lives remotely. Distractor 1 invents synchronisation across runners for local cache. Distractor 2 fabricates an org-wide layer-seeding behaviour. Distractor 3 (tar of daemon storage) was a pre-BuildKit hack — slow, fragile, and not how modern BuildKit works.

after.question: You build a Docker image in CI and want to reuse the layer cache across runs even though each runner is fresh. What pattern works?

options.correct: BuildKit with a registry-backed cache (`--cache-to type=registry --cache-from type=registry`) — layers live in a remote registry and are pulled on subsequent runs
options.distractor_1: Just push the built image to a registry each run and pull it at the start of the next build — Docker reuses the pulled image's layers as the build cache automatically, no cache flags needed
options.distractor_2: Docker Hub's persistent layer storage — every image tag pushed to Docker Hub seeds the layer cache for all future builds in the same org
options.distractor_3: Compressed tar of the Docker daemon storage directory uploaded as a build artifact — restored at the start of each subsequent run

after.explanation: Registry cache is the standard pattern: BuildKit pushes the build cache to a registry (often the same one as the image), and pulls it on the next run. The runner can be fresh because the cache lives remotely. Distractor 1 assumes pulling a previously-pushed image seeds the build cache for free — but BuildKit won't treat a pulled image as cache unless you point `--cache-from` at it (or built it with inline cache); a plain pull doesn't populate the layer cache. Distractor 2 fabricates an org-wide layer-seeding behaviour. Distractor 3 (tar of daemon storage) was a pre-BuildKit hack — slow, fragile, and not how modern BuildKit works.

distractor_self_check.real_misconception: A common belief that push-then-pull gives layer caching for free; BuildKit needs an explicit --cache-from (or inline cache) to reuse a pulled image's layers.

rewrites.change_summary: swap d2 (fabricated MaxSessionDuration=600s, below the real 3600s floor) -> aud-vs-sub OIDC misconception; d3 (MFA-inheritance, verified-FP) left BYTE-IDENTICAL per Stephen ruling

before.question: Your OIDC trust policy between GitHub Actions and AWS allows AssumeRole. What condition should you add to prevent any other repo or branch from using the role?

options.correct: A StringEquals or StringLike condition on `token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub` that pins the role to your repo and a specific branch or environment
options.distractor_1: An IP-allow condition restricting the AssumeRole call to GitHub's published runner IP ranges so only their infrastructure can assume the role
options.distractor_2: A MaxSessionDuration of 600 seconds, so even if another workflow assumed the role the session would expire before damage could be done
options.distractor_3: An MFA-required condition (`aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent: true`) on the role, since GitHub-issued JWTs include an implicit MFA claim derived from the user's authenticated GitHub session at workflow start

before.explanation: The `sub` claim is what makes OIDC trust scoped — without a condition on it, any repo with an OIDC connection to the same AWS account could assume the role. Pin to `repo:org/repo:ref:refs/heads/main` or environment-specific sub formats. Distractor 1 (IP) drifts every time GitHub adds runners and is brittle. Distractor 2 (short duration) limits damage but doesn't prevent assumption. Distractor 3 invents an MFA claim in GitHub OIDC tokens that doesn't exist.

after.question: Your OIDC trust policy between GitHub Actions and AWS allows AssumeRole. What condition should you add to prevent any other repo or branch from using the role?

options.correct: A StringEquals or StringLike condition on `token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub` that pins the role to your repo and a specific branch or environment
options.distractor_1: An IP-allow condition restricting the AssumeRole call to GitHub's published runner IP ranges so only their infrastructure can assume the role
options.distractor_2: An `aud` (audience) condition requiring the token's audience to equal `sts.amazonaws.com`, which ties the role to your repository's OIDC identity
options.distractor_3: An MFA-required condition (`aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent: true`) on the role, since GitHub-issued JWTs include an implicit MFA claim derived from the user's authenticated GitHub session at workflow start

after.explanation: The `sub` claim is what makes OIDC trust scoped — without a condition on it, any repo with an OIDC connection to the same AWS account could assume the role. Pin to `repo:org/repo:ref:refs/heads/main` or environment-specific sub formats. Distractor 1 (IP) drifts every time GitHub adds runners and is brittle. Distractor 2 pins the `aud` claim — but GitHub issues the same `sts.amazonaws.com` audience to every repository, so it can't distinguish yours; only a `sub` condition scopes the trust. Distractor 3 invents an MFA claim in GitHub OIDC tokens that doesn't exist.

distractor_self_check.real_misconception: Confusing the aud claim with the sub claim is a classic OIDC mistake; the audience is identical across all GitHub repos, so it can't scope a role to one repository.
OFF-LIMITS / verified-FP per Stephen ruling: MFA-inheritance is a genuine at-bar misconception; left byte-identical, NOT touched.

rewrites.change_summary: swap d1 (invented '10 manifest ops/min' rate limit) -> 'kubectl can't preview changes' misconception

before.question: Your GHA workflow deploys to EKS by running `kubectl apply -f manifests/`. What's the main downside compared to using Helm or kustomize?

options.correct: kubectl apply has no native concept of releases, rollbacks, or templating across environments — you end up scripting around it for non-trivial deploys
options.distractor_1: kubectl apply is rate-limited at 10 manifest operations per minute, while Helm batches its calls into a single API call
options.distractor_2: kubectl apply doesn't support secrets at all; Helm has a `helm secrets` subcommand that handles them natively
options.distractor_3: kubectl apply runs synchronously and cannot return until every resource is healthy, blocking the workflow indefinitely

before.explanation: Raw kubectl is fine for simple deploys but lacks release management — each apply is independent, with no built-in template-per-environment, no `helm history`, no `helm rollback`. Distractor 1 invents an API rate limit on kubectl. Distractor 2 fabricates a `helm secrets` subcommand (it's a third-party plugin) and misstates kubectl secret support. Distractor 3 inverts the behaviour — `kubectl apply` returns immediately by default; `--wait` is opt-in. Most teams pick Helm or kustomize specifically for the templating + release-management combination.

before.question: A pod's response time spikes from 50ms to 500ms intermittently. CloudWatch shows no CPU, memory, or network saturation. What's a common K8s-specific cause worth checking?

options.correct: CPU throttling at the limit — the pod hits its cpu limit before saturating the node, so CloudWatch sees idle resources while the pod is throttled
options.distractor_1: kubelet OOM tracking — even sub-limit pods are throttled when the node's overall memory approaches 90%, regardless of the pod's individual usage profile
options.distractor_2: Container runtime resource isolation — runc periodically pauses containers to refresh cgroups, causing latency spikes invisible to host metrics
options.distractor_3: Service mesh sidecar latency — Istio adds ~450ms of fixed per-request overhead once installed, which closely matches the observed spike pattern and is invisible to CloudWatch by default

before.explanation: CPU throttling at the container's cpu limit is invisible at the node level — node CPU may show 30% but the pod is throttled because it hit its quota in the cgroup's cfs scheduler. Container-level metrics (cgroup throttled time, kubelet's `container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total`) show this; node-level CloudWatch metrics don't. Distractor 1 invents a node-memory-driven throttle. Distractor 2 fabricates a runc pause mechanism. Distractor 3 over-states Istio overhead (typically 1-10ms per hop, not 450ms).

after.question: A pod's response time spikes from 50ms to 500ms intermittently. CloudWatch shows no CPU, memory, or network saturation. What's a common K8s-specific cause worth checking?

options.correct: CPU throttling at the limit — the pod hits its cpu limit before saturating the node, so CloudWatch sees idle resources while the pod is throttled
options.distractor_1: kubelet OOM tracking — even sub-limit pods are throttled when the node's overall memory approaches 90%, regardless of the pod's individual usage profile
options.distractor_2: Container runtime resource isolation — runc periodically pauses containers to refresh cgroups, causing latency spikes invisible to host metrics
options.distractor_3: HPA scaling events — each time the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler adds a replica, the Service briefly pauses in-flight requests while its endpoints are updated, producing the periodic spikes

after.explanation: CPU throttling at the container's cpu limit is invisible at the node level — node CPU may show 30% but the pod is throttled because it hit its quota in the cgroup's cfs scheduler. Container-level metrics (cgroup throttled time, kubelet's `container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total`) show this; node-level CloudWatch metrics don't. Distractor 1 invents a node-memory-driven throttle. Distractor 2 fabricates a runc pause mechanism. Distractor 3 blames HPA scaling — but adding a replica only appends endpoints; it doesn't pause or reroute in-flight requests, so scaling events don't produce per-request latency spikes.

distractor_self_check.real_misconception: A plausible belief that autoscaling interrupts traffic during endpoint updates; endpoint additions are non-disruptive to in-flight requests.

rewrites.change_summary: swap d1 (invented --severity/--realtime flags) -> -p crit priority-level confusion; swap d3 (invented 'systemctl follow') -> journalctl|tail -f composition misconception

before.question: You want to follow logs from nginx in real-time, filtering only entries with priority error or worse. Which command?

options.correct: `journalctl -u nginx -f -p err`
options.distractor_1: `journalctl -u nginx --follow --severity=error --realtime`
options.distractor_2: `tail -f /var/log/nginx/error.log | grep -E '^[0-9]{4}/'`
options.distractor_3: `systemctl follow nginx --errors-only`

before.explanation: journalctl uses short flags: `-f` for follow (like tail -f), `-p err` for priority filter (uses syslog priority levels: emerg, alert, crit, err, warning, notice, info, debug). Distractor 1 invents long flags (--severity, --realtime) that don't exist. Distractor 2 reads only nginx's own log file, missing journald-only entries. Distractor 3 fabricates a `systemctl follow` subcommand. Priority filtering is a heavy hitter for noise reduction in incident-response workflows.

after.question: You want to follow logs from nginx in real-time, filtering only entries with priority error or worse. Which command?

options.correct: `journalctl -u nginx -f -p err`
options.distractor_1: `journalctl -u nginx -f -p crit`
options.distractor_2: `tail -f /var/log/nginx/error.log | grep -E '^[0-9]{4}/'`
options.distractor_3: `journalctl -u nginx -p err | tail -f`

after.explanation: journalctl uses short flags: `-f` for follow (like tail -f), `-p err` for priority filter (uses syslog priority levels: emerg, alert, crit, err, warning, notice, info, debug). Distractor 1 uses real flags but the wrong level — `-p crit` shows crit/alert/emerg and silently drops the `err` level the task needs; 'error or worse' starts at `-p err`. Distractor 2 reads only nginx's own log file, missing journald-only entries. Distractor 3 pipes a non-following journalctl into `tail -f` — but journalctl without `-f` prints existing entries and exits, so `tail -f` just follows a stream that has already closed; real-time needs journalctl's own `-f`. Priority filtering is a heavy hitter for noise reduction in incident-response workflows.

distractor_self_check.real_misconception: Priority-level confusion: a junior may pick `crit` thinking it's 'error or worse,' not realising it excludes the err level.
A common shell misconception that piping into `tail -f` adds real-time following; journalctl needs its own -f.

rewrites.change_summary: swap d2 (invented terraform_module_version: field) -> 'version argument on a Git module' misconception

before.question: Your module's `main.tf` calls a Git-sourced module: `source = "git::https://github.com/acme/tf-vpc.git"`. What's missing for production use?

options.correct: A `ref=` query parameter pinning to a specific tag or commit; without it Terraform always pulls the default branch and you can't control upgrades
options.distractor_1: An explicit `provider:` block mapping the module's providers; Git-sourced modules cannot inherit providers from the calling configuration
options.distractor_2: A `terraform_module_version:` field in versions.tf declaring the minimum compatible Terraform CLI version for the Git source
options.distractor_3: An access token in the URL; Git-sourced modules require an HTTPS token to be embedded in the source string for Terraform to authenticate to private or public repositories alike

before.explanation: Without `?ref=v1.2.0`, the module floats on whatever the default branch is right now — a non-reproducible source that breaks reruns. Pinning is mandatory in production. Distractor 1 misstates provider inheritance; Git-sourced modules inherit providers fine. Distractor 2 fabricates a configuration field. Distractor 3 over-states auth requirements; public Git modules work without tokens, and private ones use either SSH keys or HTTPS tokens via standard Git mechanisms, not in the URL.

after.question: Your module's `main.tf` calls a Git-sourced module: `source = "git::https://github.com/acme/tf-vpc.git"`. What's missing for production use?

options.correct: A `ref=` query parameter pinning to a specific tag or commit; without it Terraform always pulls the default branch and you can't control upgrades
options.distractor_1: An explicit `provider:` block mapping the module's providers; Git-sourced modules cannot inherit providers from the calling configuration
options.distractor_2: A `version` argument in the module block (e.g. `version = "~> 1.2.0"`) to constrain which release of the Git module Terraform pulls
options.distractor_3: An access token in the URL; Git-sourced modules require an HTTPS token to be embedded in the source string for Terraform to authenticate to private or public repositories alike

after.explanation: Without `?ref=v1.2.0`, the module floats on whatever the default branch is right now — a non-reproducible source that breaks reruns. Pinning is mandatory in production. Distractor 1 misstates provider inheritance; Git-sourced modules inherit providers fine. Distractor 2 reaches for the `version` argument — real, but it only works for registry modules; for a `git::` source Terraform rejects it, and you must pin with `?ref=` instead. Distractor 3 over-states auth requirements; public Git modules work without tokens, and private ones use either SSH keys or HTTPS tokens via standard Git mechanisms, not in the URL.

distractor_self_check.real_misconception: Using the version argument on a Git-sourced module is a common mistake; version constraints apply only to registry modules, while Git sources pin with ?ref=.

rewrites.change_summary: swap d3 (invented --ami-from-packer flag) -> aws_ami_copy, a real resource misapplied as the Packer handoff

before.question: Your team uses Packer + Terraform. How does Terraform consume the AMI Packer produced?

options.correct: A data source (e.g. `data "aws_ami"`) queries for the latest AMI matching the team's name/tag filters, and that ID is used in the EC2/ASG resource
options.distractor_1: Packer writes the AMI ID into a shared S3 bucket that Terraform reads as part of its remote state backend
options.distractor_2: Packer creates a Terraform module containing the AMI ID, which is published to the registry and referenced via `module "image"`
options.distractor_3: Terraform's `--ami-from-packer` CLI flag tells the apply to fetch the latest Packer build directly from the build pipeline

before.explanation: The standard handshake is via data source: query AWS for AMIs matching name patterns / tags that Packer applied, sort by creation date, use the latest. This keeps the two tools coupled only through AWS metadata. Distractor 1 invents a shared-state mechanism. Distractor 2 fabricates a Packer-to-module pipeline. Distractor 3 invents a CLI flag. The data-source approach is robust because it gracefully handles AMI updates without code changes.

after.question: Your team uses Packer + Terraform. How does Terraform consume the AMI Packer produced?

options.correct: A data source (e.g. `data "aws_ami"`) queries for the latest AMI matching the team's name/tag filters, and that ID is used in the EC2/ASG resource
options.distractor_1: Packer writes the AMI ID into a shared S3 bucket that Terraform reads as part of its remote state backend
options.distractor_2: Packer creates a Terraform module containing the AMI ID, which is published to the registry and referenced via `module "image"`
options.distractor_3: An `aws_ami_copy` resource that imports the Packer-built AMI into your Terraform state, after which you reference it by ID

after.explanation: The standard handshake is via data source: query AWS for AMIs matching name patterns / tags that Packer applied, sort by creation date, use the latest. This keeps the two tools coupled only through AWS metadata. Distractor 1 invents a shared-state mechanism. Distractor 2 fabricates a Packer-to-module pipeline. Distractor 3 reaches for the real `aws_ami_copy` resource — but that duplicates an existing AMI (cross-region or re-encryption); it doesn't look up a Packer build, which is what the data source does. The data-source approach is robust because it gracefully handles AMI updates without code changes.

distractor_self_check.real_misconception: aws_ami_copy is a real resource but copies/re-encrypts an AMI; a junior could mistake it for the Packer-to-Terraform handoff, which is a data-source lookup.
